one_liner: C interpreter for the BQN array language whose SIMD primitives beat a plain C loop 5-11x on CRLF-to-LF filtering.
what_it_does: CBQN is the main implementation of BQN, an APL-family array language. It runs as a REPL or script interpreter and can also be built as libcbqn (shared or static) with a C embedding API (include/bqnffi.h: bqn_init, bqn_evalCStr, bqn_call1/2, bqn_make*Vec and zero-copy bqn_direct* readers). BQN code calls C through •FFI. You write whole-array expressions such as (cr⊸≠ ∨ ·«lf⊸≠)⊸/, and each primitive runs as a precompiled native kernel, so it does not replace a C library: you adopt a language or embed an interpreter.
how_it_is_fast: Each primitive dispatches at run time on element type (packed 1-bit booleans, 1- and 2-byte chars and ints), length and data statistics into hand-written kernels. Most of these are generated as C intrinsics from the Singeli SIMD DSL. Boolean Replicate (/), the kernel behind this result, adapts its method to the mask: a sparse method when few bits are set, grouped memcpy when the mask switches rarely, otherwise a dense SIMD compress (table lookup plus shuffle on AVX2, the AVX-512 VBMI2 compress instruction on native builds). The comparisons that build the mask produce bit-packed output via SIMD compare and movemask, which clang does not generate from the scalar C loop.
when_to_use: Data-parallel filtering, selection, grouping, sorting and searching over long homogeneous arrays (hundreds to millions of elements), especially 1- or 2-byte elements such as text bytes
Text and byte-stream transforms that fit compress or mask patterns (strip characters, split, tokenise) where the C alternative is a scalar loop the compiler cannot vectorise
Prototyping a SIMD strategy before hand-writing it in C: the author uses BQN this way, and the primitive kernels in src/singeli show how each primitive is vectorised
x86-64 machines where you can build natively (make o3n) to get AVX2, BMI2 and, on AVX-512 VBMI2 CPUs, the compress-instruction paths
when_not_to_use: Small inputs: on the page BQN is slower than C below about 200 bytes (100 bytes: 0.893 vs 0.613 ns/elt) because each primitive call has overhead
Sequential, data-dependent loops, object-heavy code, wrapping fixed-width integer arithmetic (cryptography) or decimal rounding; the page names all of these as poor fits
Competing against hand-written SIMD C: the C baseline here is a portable scalar loop, and the page says specialised C is always faster
Hot paths that must exchange data with C/C++ often: bqn_make*Vec copies its input, and the page calls FFI not the fastest interface

Arrays over 2^31 elements or deeply nested data: the README warns some builtins error or give wrong results above 2^31, recursive freeing can overflow the stack (issue #129 open), and caught errors leak memory permanently

integration.form: interpreter executable, or shared/static library (libcbqn) with a C API in include/bqnffi.h
integration.dependencies: C compiler; libffi >= 3.3 for •FFI (FFI=0 drops it); C++11 compiler for the optional replxx REPL; Singeli and precompiled bytecode come as git submodules
integration.min_toolchain: gcc >= 9 or clang >= 10 (clang preferred and default); bootstraps a build-time CBQN to run build.bqn and Singeli
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE baseline by default; AVX2, BMI2 and PCLMUL via has= or native builds; AVX-512 paths only in native builds), aarch64 (NEON), generic C fallback, 32-bit x86 with SSE2, Emscripten and WASI; Linux, BSD and macOS, Windows by cross-compilation
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the embedding API has one global bqn_init() and no thread-related functions

gotchas: The README says CBQN 'does not utilize AVX-512', yet src/singeli/src/slash.singeli has AVX-512 VBMI2 and AVX-512F compress paths for Replicate. build.bqn passes no arch restriction to Singeli for native builds, so these paths are enabled there, and the page's >10x row depends on them. The has= option accepts only up to avx2 and bmi2, and a plain 'make' (o3) targets baseline x86-64, so distro packages or default builds are likely below the measured 5x AVX2 figure (not measured).

Benchmark harness checked: same LCG data, the same number of elements per timing (5e8), and C writes into a preallocated buffer while BQN allocates a fresh result each call (this favours C). At 1 CRLF per 100 bytes the mask switches more than once per 128 bytes, so CBQN takes its branchless dense SIMD compress (slash.c dispatch), not a branchy path the repeated input could train. The BQN one-liner drops a lone CR at the very end of a buffer (« shifts in 0), while the C loop keeps it. Simulating the generator shows no tested prefix ends in CR, so the outputs match.

The 35% compiler-benchmark claim (bootbench.md) is a different measurement on a Skylake i5-6200U. comp.c was built into CBQN commit 92763fa via f='-DNATIVE_COMPILER' (so probably the same native -O3 build, inferred). The two compilers use different designs, and C is faster on sources under 1 KB, where both take about 50 us.
Error throwing uses longjmp, so the GC can only run fully between REPL lines. Long-running embedded use with frequent caught errors leaks memory (README Limitations).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Halide and Futhark compile ahead of time: Halide schedules stencil and image pipelines, and Futhark targets GPUs. Pick CBQN for interactive, irregular data-movement work on CPU (filtering, grouping, selection on byte-sized data) where no compile or scheduling step is wanted. Pick Halide or Futhark for dense numeric pipelines and GPU kernels.
verified_claims_summary: Marshall Lochbaum's versusc page measured CRLF-to-LF conversion with about one CRLF per 100 bytes on a Tiger Lake i5-1135G7. A scalar C loop (clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native, branchless, unrolled 4x) ran at 0.555 ns/byte. CBQN at commit 0d2631a ran at 0.094-0.107 ns/byte from 10 KB up with an AVX2/BMI2/PCLMUL build (5.2-5.9x) and 0.051-0.054 ns/byte with a native AVX-512 build (about 10-11x up to 300 KB, 7.1x at 1 MB). BQN was slower at 100 bytes.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-10-05, 4,105 commits, 409 stars, mostly by dzaima) with no GitHub releases, so you build from the develop branch with submodules. The licence is a choice of LGPLv3, GPLv3 or MPL-2.0 (timsort MIT, Ryu Apache-2.0/BSL-1.0). The 2023 benchmark has not been re-run on current CBQN or newer compilers.
